predecessors.name: Colony of New South Wales
predecessors.text: New South Wales, from which the ACT and Jervis Bay were later cut

predecessors.name: Colony of South Australia
predecessors.text: South Australia, which then included the Northern Territory (transferred to the Commonwealth in 1911)

ledger.x: 1901: the six colonies federate as the Commonwealth of Australia.
1901: the Colony of New South Wales becomes a state of the Commonwealth.
1901: the Colony of Victoria becomes a state of the Commonwealth.
1901: the Colony of Queensland becomes a state of the Commonwealth.
1901: the Colony of South Australia becomes a state of the Commonwealth.
1901: the Colony of Western Australia becomes a state of the Commonwealth.
1901: the Colony of Tasmania becomes a state of the Commonwealth.
1906: the Territory of Papua is constituted under Australia.
1914: Australian forces seize German New Guinea.
1920: the occupation ends as the mandate begins.
1920: Australia receives the League of Nations mandate for the Territory of New Guinea, 'German New Guinea and the Bismarck Archipelago' but not Nauru or German Samoa.
1927: the seat of government moves from Melbourne to Canberra.
1936: the Australian Antarctic Territory comes into force.
1942: Japan invades the Territory of New Guinea.
1942: Japan invades the Territory of Papua.
1943: the Japanese beachheads in Papua are cleared.
1975: Papua New Guinea becomes independent from Australia.

wars.name: Occupation of German New Guinea
wars.outcome: Rabaul taken unopposed on 12 September 1914 and the German administration surrendered on 17 September; Australia held the colony under occupation until the League of Nations mandate of 17 December 1920.

wars.name: New Guinea campaign
wars.outcome: Japanese invasion of the Territory of New Guinea (23 January 1942) and Papua (21 July 1942); Allied counter-offensives from September 1942; the campaign ended on 15 August 1945 and the territories stayed Australian.

certainty.note: The continent and Tasmania are bounded by sea and the federal borders were fixed by the 1901 Constitution; the Papua-New Guinea provincial split used here is approximate.
The front lines in New Guinea moved month by month; the Japanese-held land is drawn as one contested zone (page dates only some captures).
